# On the Weight of Small Decisions

I've been thinking about how the smallest choices ripple outward in ways we never see. Like the time I decided to take a different route home and met someone who became important to me. I didn't know it then—I just felt like walking a new way.

We live as if our decisions matter enormously or not at all, rarely acknowledging the middle ground where most of life actually happens. That coffee shop visit. The text you almost sent but didn't. The moment you chose to listen instead of respond.

There's something freeing about accepting that you can't possibly know which decisions matter. It takes the pressure off constantly optimizing. You can't live in a state of perfect awareness, so you might as well be honest about the fumbling nature of existence.

What strikes me lately is how kind people are, considering how lost everyone is. We're all just making it up, pretending we understand more than we do, yet we show up for each other anyway. That seems significant.

I think about futures I'll never experience—the person I'd be if I'd chosen differently, the life waiting in each unexplored path. It's poignant and oddly humbling. There are infinite versions of me I'll never meet.

But this version, right now, is the only one doing the choosing. That's the deal. So I try to pay attention when I can, be gentle with myself when I can't, and remain open to wherever I'm actually going rather than obsessing over where I thought I'd be.
